summary: This script provides an interactive code search tool that combines ripgrep (a fast file searcher), fzf (an interactive fuzzy finder), and bat (a syntax-highlighted file viewer) to let you search code and jump directly to matches in VSCode. It first checks that all required tools are installed, then pipes ripgrep results through fzf with a live preview, and finally opens the selected result in VSCode at the exact line number.

explanations.10: This captures the operating system type (Darwin for macOS, Linux, etc.) so we can suggest the right installation command later.
explanations.12: The 'command -v' checks if a program exists in your PATH, and '>/dev/null 2>&1' silently discards any output so we only care about success or failure.
explanations.13: This prints an error message in red using ANSI color codes (the \033[0;31m part). The color codes are invisible but tell the terminal to print in red.
explanations.22: This checks for 'bat' but also accepts 'batcat' as an alternative name, because Ubuntu and Debian renamed the package to 'batcat' to avoid conflicts.
explanations.27: If any dependencies are missing, this block shows the user which installation command to run based on their OS type.
explanations.50: We're creating a variable that will hold either 'bat' or 'batcat' depending on which one is installed, so we can use it consistently later.
explanations.61: This creates a temporary file with a unique name pattern (the X's get replaced with random characters) to store fzf's selection results.
explanations.63: The '--color=always' tells ripgrep to include color codes in its output even though it's piped to fzf, and '--smart-case' means case-insensitive search unless you use uppercase letters.
explanations.67: The delimiter ':' tells fzf that colons separate the fields in ripgrep's output (file:line:match text).
explanations.68: The '--nth=3..' means fzf will only search within the third field onwards (the matched text) when you type, ignoring the file and line number.
explanations.69: The preview command shows a syntax-highlighted excerpt of the file with the matching line highlighted, using the bat viewer.
explanations.70: The preview window appears on the right side at 60% of the terminal width, and the '+{2}+3/3' positions it so the matching line appears roughly in the middle of the preview.
explanations.72: This captures fzf's exit status code so we can tell if the user cancelled (exit 130) or selected something (exit 0).
explanations.74: This reads the contents of the temp file into the 'selected' variable, which contains the line ripgrep output that the user chose.
explanations.78: This early exit handles two cases: if fzf was cancelled (non-zero exit) or if nothing was selected (empty string), we stop processing.
explanations.82: The 'sed' command strips out all ANSI color codes from the selected line, then 'cut -d: -f1' extracts just the first field (the filename).
explanations.83: Same as above but 'cut -d: -f2' extracts the second field instead, which is the line number.
explanations.89: VSCode's '--goto' flag takes a path in 'file:line' format and jumps directly to that line when opening.
